nameStory: This tiny ocean wanderer is named after William Elford Leach, a British zoologist from the early 1800s who studied seabirds. The scientific name tells its own story too — 'Hydrobates' means 'water walker' in Greek, describing how storm petrels seem to dance across the waves, while 'leucorhous' means 'white rump,' pointing to one of its key identifying features.
description: Leach's Storm-Petrel is a small, dark seabird about the size of a large swallow that spends most of its life far out at sea. These ocean nomads have sooty black-brown plumage with a distinctive white patch on their rump and long, narrow wings that help them glide effortlessly over waves. They're part of the 'tubenose' family, meaning they have special tube-shaped nostrils on top of their bills that help them smell food and navigate across vast ocean distances. You're most likely to see them during boat trips far offshore, where they appear to 'walk' on water as they pick tiny fish and plankton from the surface.

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: Look for a bright white, V-shaped patch on the lower back that's clearly visible when the bird flies away from you — it stands out like a beacon against the dark body

idTips.label: Erratic flight pattern
idTips.description: Watch for a distinctive bouncing, zigzag flight with deep wingbeats and sudden direction changes, like a bat fluttering over water rather than steady gliding

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About swallow-sized with long, narrow, angled wings and a slightly forked tail that gives it a delicate, angular silhouette against the sky

idTips.label: Water dancing behavior
idTips.description: Appears to walk or hop across the water surface with legs dangling down, patting the waves with their feet while picking at tiny floating food

idTips.label: Dark overall coloring
idTips.description: Sooty black-brown all over except for the white rump, looking almost charcoal-colored with a slightly lighter brown tone on the wing coverts

habitat: In New England waters, you'll find Leach's Storm-Petrels far offshore in deep ocean waters, typically 20+ miles from land where the continental shelf drops off. They prefer areas with upwelling currents that bring tiny fish, squid, and plankton to the surface. While they don't breed in New England, they pass through our waters during migration, especially in late summer and fall.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters during spring migration, though a few may pass through offshore areas in May as they head to northern breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Occasional sightings during summer pelagic birding trips, especially in July and August when some non-breeding birds or failed breeders wander south from Canadian colonies.
seasonality.fall: Peak viewing time from late August through October when birds migrate south past New England's offshore waters, often visible during boat trips to fishing grounds.
seasonality.winter: Generally absent from New England waters, having continued south to tropical and subtropical oceans where they spend the winter months.

funFact: Leach's Storm-Petrels are so committed to avoiding daytime predators at their breeding colonies that they actually delay nesting until fall in northern Norway, waiting out the midnight sun of Arctic summer when there's literally no darkness to hide their arrival at night!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Wilson's Storm-Petrel, but Leach's has a forked tail (Wilson's is square), more erratic flight (Wilson's glides more steadily), and yellow webbing between the toes instead of Wilson's black webbing — though you'd need binoculars and luck to see the feet! Memory trick: 'Leach's goes left and right' with its zigzag flight pattern.
contextualKnowledge: These birds are sometimes called 'Mother Carey's Chickens' by sailors, after a legendary sea spirit, and seeing them was considered both good luck and a sign of approaching storms. Despite being called 'petrels,' they're not closely related to the larger petrel species but belong to their own distinct family of storm-petrels.
compareHints: Leach's Storm-Petrel differs from its close relative the Band-rumped Storm-Petrel by having a more deeply forked tail and more erratic, bat-like flight pattern, while Band-rumped flies more steadily with shallower wingbeats. Leach's also has a slightly more pronounced white rump patch that extends further up the back, and tends to hold its wings more angled when gliding compared to Band-rumped's straighter wing position.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Leach's Storm-Petrel (the only other species in the same genus found in New England), Band-rumped Storm-Petrel has a complete white rump band rather than a divided one, and flies with more gliding and less erratic fluttering.
